content: Calcium phosphate refers to a group of minerals that contain calcium ions (Ca2+) combined with orthophosphates (PO43−), metaphosphates, or pyrophosphates (P2O74−), and sometimes hydrogen or hydroxide ions. It is the primary form of calcium found in bovine milk and blood. Approximately 70% of bone is composed of hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral also known as bone mineral. Tooth enamel is made up of nearly 90% hydroxyapatite. The solubility of calcium phosphate decreases as temperature increases, which is an unusual property compared to most other compounds. When heated, calcium phosphate precipitates out of solution. In milk, calcium phosphate exists in higher concentrations than would normally be possible at its natural pH because it is present in a colloidal form. This colloidal calcium phosphate (CCP) is bound to casein protein along with magnesium, zinc, and citrate. Calcium phosphate is utilized in the production of phosphoric acid and fertilizers, such as in the Odda process. However, excessive use of certain forms of calcium phosphate can result in nutrient-rich runoff, leading to environmental issues like algal blooms and eutrophication. In the food industry, calcium phosphate is used as the acidic component in leavening agents, identified by the E number E341. It is also an ingredient in cheese products. A supersaturated calcium phosphate solution, such as Caphosol, is employed in the prevention and treatment of oral mucositis caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Tricalcium phosphate is used as a nutritional supplement and is naturally present in cow milk. However, the most commonly used and cost-effective calcium supplements are calcium carbonate (which should be taken with food) and calcium citrate (which can be taken without food). Hydroxyapatite has been studied to a limited extent as a food supplement, and its use is generally discouraged. In dentistry, calcium phosphate is incorporated into various products to promote remineralization. It is also used as a diluent in some medications, where it can impart a grey color to tablets in the absence of additional coloring agents. Another application of calcium phosphate is in gene transfection, where it forms a complex with DNA, facilitating the DNA's entry into cells. Additionally, calcium phosphate is being explored in the development of contrast agents for medical imaging. Several forms of calcium phosphate exist, including: Monocalcium phosphate (E341(i)): Ca(H2PO4)2 Dicalcium phosphate (dibasic calcium phosphate, E341(ii)): CaHPO4 Tricalcium phosphate (tribasic calcium phosphate, E341(iii)): Ca3(PO4)2, often referred to simply as calcium phosphate or calcium orthophosphate Hydroxyapatite: Ca5(PO4)3(OH) Apatite: Ca10(PO4)6(OH, F, Cl, Br)2 Octacalcium phosphate: Ca8H2(PO4)6·5H2O Biphasic calcium phosphate: A biomaterial composed of a mixture of tricalcium phosphate and hydroxyapatite. It is used as an alternative to bone grafting around osseous implants, such as dental implants. Over time, it resorbs and is replaced by new bone through the process of bone regeneration. Tetracalcium phosphate: Ca4(PO4)2O Amorphous calcium phosphate: A glassy precipitate with variable composition that may occur in biological systems. Calcium phosphate is also listed in the British Pharmacopoeia, indicating its recognized status in pharmaceutical and medical applications.
